content: Dock10, also referred to as Zizimin3, is a large protein with a molecular weight of approximately 240 kDa. It plays a role in intracellular signaling pathways and belongs to the DOCK-D subfamily of the DOCK family of guanine nucleotide exchange factors (GEFs). These GEFs are responsible for activating small G proteins. Dock10 was discovered through bioinformatics methods as part of a family of evolutionarily conserved proteins, known as the DOCK family, which exhibit significant sequence similarity. It is expressed in various tissues, including peripheral blood leukocytes, the brain, spleen, lung, and thymus. The structural organization of Dock10 is consistent with other members of the DOCK-D/Zizimin subfamily, sharing a high degree of sequence similarity. It contains a DHR2 domain, which is involved in binding small G proteins, and a DHR1 domain, which in some DOCK family proteins interacts with membrane phospholipids. Additionally, Dock10 has an N-terminal PH domain, which, in the case of Dock9/Zizimin1, facilitates recruitment to the plasma membrane. The DHR2 domain of Dock10 has been shown to bind to small G proteins such as Cdc42, TC10, and TCL, although these interactions are characterized by low affinity. The physiological role of Dock10 remains poorly understood. However, research in lymphocytes has demonstrated that Dock10 expression is upregulated in B-lymphocytes and Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia (CLL) cells in response to the cytokine IL-4. This finding suggests that Dock10 may play a role in B-cell activation and proliferation. Furthermore, another study identified Dock10 as a protein that is overexpressed in certain aggressive forms of papillary thyroid carcinoma.
